title: The average that never settles
hook: Average enough data and it settles on a number. Always? Here is one that won't.

knows: that running averages of die rolls settle (law of large numbers)
doesNotKnow: that the law of large numbers needs a finite mean
heavy-tailed distributions whose rare giant values dominate

misconception: Averaging more data always settles on a stable number.
objective: The learner can explain that when rare giant values are common enough (a heavy tail such as the Cauchy), one draw can outweigh thousands, so the running average never settles: the mean of n Cauchy draws is as spread out as one draw.

claims.text: The running average of fair die rolls settles toward 3.5.
claims.source: Strong law of large numbers; the die mean is (1+2+...+6)/6 = 3.5 and its SD 1.71, so the SD of a 10,000-roll average is 0.017.

claims.text: The average of n draws from a standard Cauchy distribution has exactly the same distribution as a single draw, so it never narrows.
claims.source: Characteristic function of the standard Cauchy is exp(-|t|); for the mean of n draws it is exp(-|t|/n)^n = exp(-|t|). W. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 2, 2nd ed. (1971), the Cauchy distribution as a stable law; chapter not checked by the builder.

claims.text: At any number of draws, the Cauchy average lands more than 1 away from 0 half the time.
claims.source: For standard Cauchy, P(|X| > 1) = 1 - (2/pi) atan(1) = 0.5, and the mean of n draws is standard Cauchy (c2). cauchyTail() in src/demos/probability/average-that-never-settles/model.ts. Re-run: in 400 seeds, |mean at 10,000| > 1 in 49.75%; die average more than 0.05 from 3.5 in 0.75%.

claims.text: The stage draws five seeded runs at a time. In the first five, after 11,000 draws the die averages are between 3.455 and 3.534 and the Cauchy averages between -0.09 and 2.57; in the next five, die 3.487 to 3.503 and Cauchy -1.94 to 1.68.
claims.source: batchRuns() / runs() in model.ts, seed 1853, untuned (the first seed tried); draws by inverse CDF tan(pi(u - 1/2)). Run 0 alone: a giant draw (about 33,000) just after 1,050 draws throws its average from 1.4 to about 24. Five runs per batch because a single run can look calm (run 1 stays within -2.1 to 2.8 and is at 0.12 after 5,000 draws and -0.19 after 10,000); in 200 other batches all five Cauchy averages were within 1 of 0 at 11,000 draws in only 4 (theory 0.5^5 = 3.1%). The claim about all runs is c2-c3.

claims.text: The Cauchy is a toy heavy-tailed distribution chosen because its mean does not exist.
claims.source: E|X| is infinite for the Cauchy, so the law of large numbers does not apply. Stated on the stage chip.

recall.question: You average more and more samples from a distribution with rare but enormous values (no finite mean). What happens to the average?
options: It can keep being knocked around by single huge values
recall.why: The law of large numbers needs a finite mean. When one rare draw can be bigger than all the rest combined, adding data does not tame the average.
